hypothesis: A MACD cross signals the start of a momentum move, while a mid‑range RSI (40‑60) filters out extreme overbought/oversold conditions that often lead to reversals; ATR‑based sizing and stops adapt risk to current volatility, ensuring consistent risk‑reward ratios across varying market regimes.

A wider RSI band (30-70) combined with a MACD crossover captures more momentum trades while still filtering out weak moves; ATR is used only for risk limits, not as an entry filter, ensuring trades occur in volatile conditions.

A Donchian breakout signals the start of a new trend; combining it with a moderate RSI filter confirms momentum while an ATR-based risk manager adapts stop and take levels to current volatility, yielding higher probability entries and better risk control on a 3‑minute chart.
EMA crossovers identify trend direction, while an ATR filter ensures trades are taken only in volatile periods, reducing false entries in low‑activity regimes.

A Donchian channel breakout signals a new trend direction; filtering with ADX > 25 confirms the trend strength, while ATR-based stops protect against volatility spikes. This combination should reduce false breakouts in ranging markets and provide clear exit points when the trend weakens.

EMA cross captures trend initiation while RSI between 30 and 70 filters out extreme market conditions; this combination reduces whipsaw entries in ranging markets and leverages ATR for dynamic risk sizing.
